content: Hydraulics is a branch of science and engineering that focuses on the mechanical properties of liquids. It is a subset of the broader field of fluid power. The theoretical basis for hydraulics is provided by fluid mechanics, which examines the behavior and properties of fluids, while hydraulics applies these principles to engineering and practical uses. The scope of hydraulics spans numerous scientific and engineering disciplines. It encompasses topics such as the flow of liquids through pipes, the design and construction of dams, fluid control systems, pumps, turbines, hydropower generation, computational fluid dynamics, methods for measuring fluid flow, the behavior of river channels, and the processes of erosion. The term hydraulics originates from the Greek word hydraulikos, which itself derives from hydor (meaning water) and aulos (meaning pipe). This etymology reflects the historical association of hydraulics with water and its movement through conduits. Historically, the earliest known contributors to the field of hydraulics were Ctesibius (circa 270 BCE) and Hero of Alexandria (circa 10–70 CE) in the Hellenized Greek world. In ancient China, notable figures such as Sunshu Ao (6th century BCE), Ximen Bao (5th century BCE), Du Shi (circa 31 CE), Zhang Heng (78–139 CE), and Ma Jun (200–265 CE) made significant advancements in hydraulic engineering. During medieval China, engineers like Su Song (1020–1101 CE) and Shen Kuo (1031–1095 CE) further developed hydraulic technologies. In ancient Sri Lanka, the Sinhalese civilization utilized hydraulics extensively in the kingdoms of Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa. They are credited with the invention of the valve tower, or valve pit, which was used to regulate water flow over 2,000 years ago. Large-scale irrigation systems were constructed to support agriculture, horticulture, and domestic needs. In Sigiriya, Sri Lanka, hydraulic systems were also employed for ornamental and recreational water features, surface drainage, erosion control, and cooling mechanisms. In 1619, Benedetto Castelli, a student of Galileo Galilei, published a foundational work on hydrodynamics titled Della Misura dell'Acque Correnti (On the Measurement of Running Waters). This work laid the groundwork for modern hydrodynamic studies and contributed to the management of rivers in the Papal States starting in 1626. Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) made significant contributions to the study of fluid hydrodynamics and hydrostatics. His work focused on the principles governing hydraulic fluids. Pascal invented the hydraulic press, a device that amplifies a small force applied to a smaller area into a larger force distributed over a larger area, while maintaining the same pressure throughout the system. This invention operates based on Pascal's Law, which states that in an incompressible fluid at rest, the pressure difference is proportional to the height difference. Furthermore, any change in pressure applied at one point in the fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout the entire fluid.
